subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION-AMENDMENTS RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to submit a very brief argument to Your Honour on the question which you yourself raised on the 10th of February with respect to the proper construction of standing order 60. It will be remembered that last year there was a discussion about the construction of the standing order and you, sir, expressed in the ruling you then made the view found at page 3375 of Hansard on June 18, 1952, namely:
Accordingly in my opinion the practice of the minister opening the debate on the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair for the house to consider in committee of the whole a resolution preceding a money bill should be discontinued.
Some weeks ago, when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) followed the directive contained in that ruling, it will be remembered that quite a long debate ensued both about the propriety of his doing so and about the merits of the resolution that it was proposed to refer to the committee. Following quite a long debate on that subject

you, sir, on the 10th of February, as will be found at page 1784 of Hansard, stated:
From time to time there have been discussions in the house as to whether Mr. Speaker should leave the chair without question put when the motion Is called on the second day.
That is to say, on a day following the day when the recommendation of the Governor General has been communicated to the house and a resolution has been passed that it will be considered in committee. You went on to say:
I think probably we all agreed at that time that the motion for Mr. Speaker to leave the chair was debatable. I now am not sure that we were correct [DOT]-although we all agreed. The motion, when it is first put, is that at the next sitting of the house Mr. Speaker will leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole on the resolution. That is a decision of the house-that Mr. Speaker will leave the chair at the next sitting.
If the house has reached that decision, then how can the resolution be debatable with the Speaker in the chair when that second day arrives? The house has reached that decision. I think that was a point which was not brought up on previous occasions when this matter was being considered; and it is certainly a point which was not raised on the last occasion.
Then you say:
I am satisfied that the ruling I made in June of 1952 should be revised.
I must apologize, Mr. Speaker, for not raising that point fully at that time because I think it has a very important bearing upon the proper construction of standing order 60. I want to make it quite clear that this is not an attempt to curtail debate in the house on a resolution preceding a money bill. There is ample opportunity for debating such a resolution under the terms of standing order 60 itself, but standing order 60 provides that the debate shall take place in committee. We have, 1 think, a very recent and convincing example that there is ample opportunity for debate in committee in the long debate that has been taking place in committee on the resolution that it would be advisable to introduce a bill to extend the duration of the Emergency Powers Act.
But the question arises as to when that debate should take place and in what form it should take place. Standing order 60 is an order that was adopted immediately after confederation and which in i,ts terms was founded on the similar order that existed in the parliament of Westminster. It was for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the British North America Act which provided that there would be no appropriation of money or imposition of taxes without a recommendation of His Excellency the Governor General. In order to carry out that
Standing Order 60
provision, standing order 60 was made and provides, as all members know, as follows:
If any motion be made in the house for any public aid or charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof may not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned till such further day as the house thinks fit to appoint; and then it shall be referred to a committee of the whole house, before any resolution or vote of the house do pass thereupon.
It is quite proper that with respect to all matters involving charges upon the public there should be a debate, and the standing order provides that such debate shall take place in committee before there is any decision of the house upon the subject.
What is the proper procedure? It must not be overlooked, as Your Honour pointed out on the 10th of February, that when such a resolution is called, as this resolution was called today, there is in existence a decision of the house. If hon. members will refer to Votes and Proceedings of the 15th of January, 1953, at page 136 of Votes and Proceedings, they will find the following:

subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION-AMENDMENTS RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext:
,-That the house do go into committee of the whole at the next sitting of the house to consider the following proposed resolution-
Then follow the terms of the resolution that have just been read from the table by the deputy clerk.
Whereupon, Mr. Winters, a member of the Queen's privy council, informed the house that His Excellency the Governor General, having been informed of the subject matter of the said proposed resolution, recommends it to the house.
Resolved, that the house do go into committee of the whole at the next sitting of the house to consider the said proposed resolution.
That is a decision of the house, that at the next sitting it will go into committee of the whole to consider the said proposed resolution. That decision of the house, I submit, cannot be reversed during the same session. It would not be in order to reverse that decision of the house during the same session. It is a decision that the house would go into committee to consider the resolution at the next sitting. It is well known that "next sitting" does not mean the sitting immediately following but means some sitting following the one when the resolution is adopted.
I submit that that resolution in its terms is a binding decision of the house that it will go into committee to consider the proposed resolution, and that there are then two reasons why it should not again be the subject of a debate in the house until it has been considered by the committee. The first is that, the decision having been made, it is a general principle that it cannot be called into question again during the same session. Second, the decision amounts to a reference

Standing Order 60
of the proposed resolution to a committee. It is a well-known rule of the house that when a matter is referred to a committee it is then not subject to debate in the house until the committee has made its report.
Now, the question arises as to whether when, the resolution having been called to be considered in committee, the Speaker should leave the chair without question put. Your Honour pointed out that that question had not been discussed and that it was one that had an important bearing upon the procedure followed in connection with these resolutions and money bills. It might seem that there still remained a question as to which of the next sittings would be the one when the Speaker would leave the chair; but the question, that it will be considered and debated in committee has been decided. "The next sitting of the house" does not mean a definite date. It is not as if the house had said it would go into committee on March 23 to consider this Resolution. It is "the next sitting", and that is, in parliamentary usage and practice, an indefinite date.
It might seem that there could be a discussion as to when that next sitting might be. There again, sir, I submit that there are two reasons why there can be no question about that. It has become an established and accepted practice that at the end of a day's sitting the business for the following day is announced and, if there is no dispute about it, that is the business that will be proceeded with on the following day. There is, moreover, not only a matter of practice but a positive standing order, No. 17, paragraph 2, which provides that this having become a government order, or something that goes on the order paper under the heading of government orders, on any day that government business has precedence it may be called in such sequence among government orders as the government may see fit. That is a positive standing order of the house that makes it binding on the house to consider any such order as the government may see fit to bring forward and is on the order paper among the government orders.
I do not want to insist on any autocratic or arbitrary application of that rule "and that is why the business for a following sitting is announced the night before. If there is any question about it at all I think we always try to be as accommodating as possible. But, as a matter of rule, standing order 17, paragraph 2, is there and it excludes opportunity or occasion for any debate as to whether the next sitting should be a sitting of today or of the following or any other day.

Because of these provisions I submit that when a decision has been made that the house will go into committee of the whole to consider a certain proposed resolution, that is a decision that is binding on the house and the only further question is as to when that will take place. The time when it is to take place is announced in the house and is, under standing order No. 17, subsection 2, a matter that is put by the standing order in the discretion of the government.
It seems to me that after there has been the kind of decision that was made with respect to this resolution on January 15, there must be consideration given to the resolution in committee; and there should be full debate and consideration given to it in the committee. It cannot be disposed of elsewhere. It cannot be afterwards disposed of at all until the committee has dealt with it because it has been referred to the committee, and because the standing order says there shall be no debate or vote in the house upon it until it has been considered in committee.
Now, it may be that instead of its being considered in committee it would be more appropriate to have it considered with the Speaker in the chair, but that would be a departure from time-honoured constitutional practice in the mother of parliaments and here that any charge on the people must first be considered in committee before it comes as a definite proposal to be dealt with by the house. I am not going to speculate about why that became the practice of the constitution, but it did become the practice of the constitution that members of parliament in committee would first of all consider whether or not a thing of that kind should come as a formal proposal before parliament.
I submit that the argument advanced against the proposal I am contending for, that if there was a debate it had to be an opportunity for a full debate, demonstrates that there cannot be any half measure. If there is a debate it must become in fact a debate on the merits of the proposal, and that is something which cannot be disposed of until it has had consideration in committee.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) argued very strongly that there could not be any middle course.
I think Your Honour found, in our experience on the motion in connection with the Emergency Powers Act, that this suggested half course, namely that there might be a debate on the negative of the proposal that the Speaker leave the chair, afforded no possibility of determining what would be in order and what would not be in order; and in fact that meant that if there was a debate

at all it inevitably became a full debate upon the advisability or otherwise of having that kind of measure before parliament at the present session. The hon. member pointed out that a debate on the motion that the Speaker leave the chair cannot be excluded on grounds of any mere formality.
I think he was quite correct on the ground that if parliament had decided the question against the government it would have to be considered as a vote of no confidence. I do not think there could be any clearer vote of no confidence if the government announced in the speech from the throne and recommended a resolution of that character, and the house refused even to consider it. I do not think there could be any clearer demonstration that the government would have lost the confidence of the house. It may be that things could be put before parliament on the recommendation of the government, be debated, and' the government could change its mind and withdraw them; but if the government comes before parliament to carry out an announcement in the speech from the throne, recommending that something receive consideration, and parliament decides it will not get consideration, then that is a formal, categorical declaration that the government no longer has the confidence of the house.
So it is not just a formality, I submit, that proper construction of the standing order requires that there be a decision about whether it will go into committee or not. When that decision has been made, then it becomes a government order and it can be called after observing proper, courteous practices and when it is called, there is no motion required that the Speaker leave the chair. There is nothing further to do but to carry out the decision previously recorded, previously made, and appearing on the Votes and Proceedings-that that bit of the government orders will be considered in the committee of the whole.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my understanding of the situation was very much the same as that which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) gave in the summary with which he opened his remarks, that is the summary of the circumstances which have given rise to this discussion on the point of order concerning the application of standing order No. 60.
It was my understanding, accordingly, that Your Honour had indicated earlier in this session that, with respect to your ruling of June, 1952, that limited discussion only would be allowed, confined to the negative of the proposition that the Speaker leave the chair, that ruling was found to be impossible of application. We are, therefore, now considering anew the question: should any debate at all be allowed at this stage of the resolution. It was to that subject which the Prime Minister addressed his remarks this afternoon, and it is on that point which I understand, and I hope, Your Honour has invited argument today.
If that be the case, then may I just preface what I have to say with the assertion that it seems to me there will be no disagreement that the rules, of which we are now discussing one standing order, were designed carefully to preserve the rights of debate. Standing order No. 38 clearly lays down the motions which are debatable and was drawn for the purpose of preserving the rights of debate. It seems to me that is the issue before us in the point of order which is being discussed.
Having said that, and having indicated I approach it from that point of view, I think it should be made clear also that at no time have we asserted on this side of the house, and I do not myself now assert, that we will as a matter of course debate every such resolution with the Speaker in the chair. Your Honour will recall that a number of such resolutions have come before the house and have been allowed to pass; Your Honour left the chair and immediately the discussion took place in the committee. I think it would be safe to say that in connection with the resolution which we have before us now there would not be any discussion with Your Honour in the chair, except that this has been chosen as the vehicle to debate this point of order. There have been a number of such resolutions when the opposition has allowed the resolution to go through and the discussion took place in committee. I want to make

Standing Order 60
it clear that I hope we will not be taken as asserting that we insist on debating each resolution with the Speaker in the chair. We assert, rather, that the rules of the house, properly interpreted, give the opposition-or government members for that matter-the right to debate every such resolution while Your Honour is still in the chair, whether the right is always exercised or not.
Then, Mr. Speaker, as to the argument as to what standing order No. 60 actually permits, I should like to deal with that under three headings: First, the rule itself, as read in conjunction with standing order No. 38; second, the light which is thrown on the question by the fact that the British House of Commons now has a clear and specific rule to an exactly opposite effect- and I shall submit that the fact that they have a rule that specifically states there shall be no debate at this point is a clear indication that the fact we have no such rule means that a debate can be permitted at this stage in this house; third, I should like to refer Your Honour to a precedent which I shall suggest establishes clearly that there is a right to debate a resolution in this house with Your Honour in the chair.
Before coming to my main argument under those three headings, may I just deal briefly with the argument put forward by the Prime Minister this afternoon? If I followed him correctly, he stated that there should ibe no debate on the motion at this stage because there has been a decision of the house already that the house should go into committee on this resolution. If I understood him correctly the Prime Minister said that, since there was a decision of the house on the matter, it was not logical nor proper that a debate should take place as to whether, in fact, Your Honour should leave the chair for the house to go into committee. With respect, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the Prime Minister has not fully stated the position. The question is not now on the resolution on which that earlier decision was taken; the question is now on the motion arising out of that earlier decision, the motion that the Speaker leave the chair. It is true that a decision of the house was taken on an earlier occasion, but the implementation of that decision now requires a further motion and that is the motion which is put, that the Speaker do now leave the chair.

the house to resolve itself into committee on the said resolution." Under our rules, such a motion is clearly debatable. I submit to you, sir, that the Prime Minister's argument is met when we think for a moment of the similarity between this procedure on a resolution and the procedure on a bill. It is true that when we have first reading of a bill it is merely a formality. The bill is read the first time. Then, if I am not mistaken, you will recall that Your Honour puts the words, "When shall this bill be read a second time?" The house agrees and decides that it will be read "at the next sitting of the house". Your Honour uses the words, "next sitting", and then I think goes on to say that this bill will be read at the next sitting of the house.
Now, that being the case, to deal with the line of reasoning which the Prime Minister followed, that there has been a decision of the house that the bill will be read a second time at the next sitting-and it is, as the Prime Minister has said, one of those matters of government business on which the government decides when it will next be proceeded with, subject to informal discussion as to the actual time of calling it-it certainly does not follow, as the Prime Minister argued in connection with the resolution, that, because the house has decided the bill will be read a second time at its next sitting, the formal motion for second reading would be carried without debate.

speechtext: May I just interrupt the hon. member to point out that under standing order No. 38, paragraph (d), the second reading of a bill is debatable. The rule provides for debate on the motion for second reading.

speechtext:
Yes, it certainly does, and that is my pointy I am seeking to illustrate the point by pointing out the parallel between the procedure on a resolution and a bill, and dealing with the argument of the Prime Minister which he says should be carried to the conclusion, in the case of a resolution, that the decision of the house having been taken on a previous occasion that the resolution will be considered later in committee, the subsequent motion to leave the chair is not debatable because, he says, a decision of the house has already been taken. But I am pointing out-and- as Your Honour has emphasized-that our standing orders provide clearly that although that same decision has been taken in the case of a bill, that it will be read the second time at the next sitting, nevertheless the actual motion for second reading is debatable.
I therefore think that is the answer to the Prime Minister's argument. The house has in fact made the decision but the motion

arising out of that decision is still debatable in the case of a bill; and my submission is that a similar motion arising out of the earlier decision of the house in connection with a resolution is similarly debatable. I base my opinion on rule 38.

I meant on that particular question. I think Your Honour indicates that your opinion would be that the motion is for the second reading to be considered at a later sitting. My opinion is that the words Your Honour uses indicate clearly that the decision of the house is that a bill will be called for second reading at the next sitting in the same way as the decision of the house on a resolution is that the house will call the motion to go into committee on the said resolution at the next sitting.
I now come back to the point that, just as in the case of a bill the second reading requires a further motion, so in the case of the resolution the consideration in committee requires a further motion and, I submit, both motions are debatable. As I said, I base that opinion on three branches of the argument which I should like to put forward. The first is on the plain meaning of the rule of our house itself.
Under standing order 38 the following principle is spelled out:
(1)	The following motions are debatable:- Every motion
(a) standing on the order of proceedings for the day, (except government notices of motion for the house to go into committee at a later date).
Then there are a number of other subparagraphs under that heading, and then we find paragraph 2 which reads:
(2)	All other motions, including adjournment motions, shall be decided without debate or amendment.
Standing Order 60
To go back to rule 38 (1) (a), this motion that the Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee on the said resolution is clearly a motion standing on the order paper. It is like every other motion on the order paper and, spelled out, this motion has three ingredients: (a) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair; (b) for the house to go into committee of the whole; (c) for the purpose of considering the resolution that it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide so and so, in the words of the resolution.
Under the application of this Canadian rule Your Honour will, I think, agree that it would have been open to the house to debate the motion to go into committee of supply, even on Thursdays and Fridays, unless we had the specific exception provided by the rules, which says that the motion for the house to resolve itself into committee of supply shall not be debatable on Thursdays and Fridays.
The motion to go into committee of supply is exactly the same in form as the motion now before the house in connection with this resolution. It is a resolution by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), on which that minister moves "that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of supply for the purpose of considering the supply to be granted to Her Majesty". It is in exactly the same form as the motion made by the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters)- the motion which it is necessary for him to make-"that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole to consider the resolution that it is expedient to introduce" such and such a measure. They are two identical motions. Yet in order to prevent debate on the supply motion on Thursdays and Fridays we have to have a specific rule saying that there shall be no debate. We have no such rule in connection with a general motion for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole on a money resolution. I submit that the argument-I think it is called per contra-indicates clearly that if it takes a specific rule to prohibit debate in the one case, then the absence of that specific rule means clearly that debate is allowed in the other case.

Standing Order 60
It is not permitted to an hon. member to discuss what will be considered when the house does go into committee of supply; whereas if the motion on so-called money resolutions is' debated, then the house is debating, with the Speaker in the chair, what will be debated when the house is in committee of the whole, a procedure which is not allowed on a motion for the house to resolve itself into committee of supply.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect may I suggest that we are likely to get confused between two things if we follow your suggestion any further. What we are discussing here is the question of whether or not a motion is debatable, not what we can discuss in the course of that debate. I think that is a separate question. As an argument in support of my contention that the motion is debatable, I am using the fact that to prevent debate on the similar motion to go into supply, we require, and the rules provide, a special prohibitory rule. I therefore say that fact argues clearly that, if it takes a rule to prohibit us from debating the motion to go into supply on Thursday and Friday, the fact that there is no such specific rule prohibiting debate on this motion means that the motion is debatable.
To deal perhaps more closely with the point which was just made by Your Honour, may I say I noticed that Your Honour did not suggest that the motion to go into supply was not debatable except on Thursday and Friday. There is no such suggestion. That motion is debatable. I submit it is debatable in the same way as this motion is debatable. It is open to any hon. member to advance reasons why the house should not go into committee of supply or to put forward any matter which he thinks it is desirable for him to put forward; and he can advance any reason that he can think of why the house should not go into committee of supply in accordance with the motion made by the minister; that is, except on Thursdays and Fridays when debate is specifically prohibited. Therefore, following that argument, on this motion to go into committee of the whole on a resolution, it is open to any member to advance any reason why the house should not go into committee of the whole to consider that resolution. I submit that the two are absolutely on all fours. And the fact that it takes a specific rule to preclude debate on the motion for committee of supply on Thursdays and Fridays, and that there is no such rule precluding debate on a resolution, is the clearest proof that, in fact, debate on the motion for committee on a resolution is allowed under our rules.

I think it is necessary in considering this matter to remember this, that what we are claiming the right to debate is not the resolution itself. The resolution is not before the house. What is before the house is the motion that Your Honour leave the chair for the house to go into committee of the whole. And it is that motion we debate and that, in my submission, we are as free to debate as we are to debate a motion on Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday for Your Honour to leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply. The two are on all fours.

speechtext: Does the hon. member suggest that the debate should be as wide on the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair on a money resolution as on a motion to go into supply? I am sure the hon. member has in mind that it is grievances that can be discussed on going into supply.

subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION-AMENDMENTS RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext:
I hope I have not used words which might be taken to indicate that debate might be as wide on one occasion as on the other. I said that in the same way as one is a debatable motion, except on Thursdays and Fridays, so is the other. And it is open to any hon. member, within the rules of relevancy, to bring forward reasons why the house should not go into committee on the resolution, just as it is open to hon. members within the rules of debate to bring forward reasons why the house should not go into committee of supply on the other motion.
Then, leaving that for the time being, I should like to outline briefly another branch of the argument, which is based on the position in the British house. The British equivalent of our standing order 60 is their standing order 83, which is found at page 46 of the 1950 edition of the Standing Orders of the British House of Commons. That order states as follows:
If any motion be made in the house for any aid, grant or charge upon the public revenue, whether payable out of the consolidated revenue or out of money to be provided by parliament, or for any charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof shall not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned until such further day as the house shall think fit to appoint; and then it shall be referred to a committee of the whole house before any resolution or vote of the house do pass therein.
Those last words-at least, the import of them-are exactly the same as the words in our standing order 60, which we are now discussing. However, the position is that in Great Britain the resolution preceding a money bill, by another rule of the British house, is rendered not subject to debate. The rule is clear and specific on the point. It says that there shall be no debate. Rule 17(1) of the British house states:
Whenever an order of the day is read for the house to resolve itself into a committee other

than a committee on a bill, Mr. Speaker shall leave the chair without putting any question, and the house shall thereupon resolve itself into such committee-
That is the relevant portion. So that under British procedure now prevailing they have a standing order which specifically precludes debate on a motion for committee on a resolution such as we have before us. And if it took a specific standing order in the British house to preclude debate; and if, as the Prime Minister himself said, our standing order No. 60 was one the object of which was to adopt the general British practice on motions; then I submit that the significant omission of the specific standing order 17 of the British house, which prohibits debate on this resolution, is another very strong argument in favour of the proposition that, in the absence of such a prohibition, obviously, free debate is intended and must be allowed.
The summary of the argument here is, surely, that where our two practices are based upon the same starting point, namely, the preservation of the freedom of debate, and where both have an order which says, in general terms, that almost all motions standing on the orders of the day shall be debatable; and where in the British house, as set out in their standing order 17, they make an exception of a motion on a resolution preceding a money bill, and where we do not make that exception: then obviously our rules were designed and framed with the intention of permitting debate at this stage, on the resolution preceding a money bill; because if we had not intended to permit it we would have adopted the same standing order as has the British House of Commons under its rule 17.
Then the third branch of my argument deals with the suggestion made that this is a purely formal motion, and to some extent it comes back to the argument advanced earlier this afternoon by the Prime Minister. As I tried to indicate, although it is true that to some extent there has been a decision of the house that the further consideration of this resolution will take place on another day, it is still necessary that there should be a motion to implement that decision of the house. And that is the motion which the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) is now making-that Mr. Speaker do leave the chair.
It has been suggested that it is carrying things to an absurd point to say that the house should debate what has been described as a purely procedural motion, and which it is suggested in the Prime Minister's argument would mean that the house is trying to upset its own previous decision. I suggest that every time we have a debate at any subsequent stage in a bill we are doing exactly
Standing Order 60
that. We are reopening the question as to the merits of the measure upon which the house has made a previous decision.
And what is the occasion of that debate? The occasion of that debate in every case is a further motion, a new motion, either that Mr. Speaker do leave the chair for the house to go into committee, or that the bill be read a second time, or whatever the motion may be. But under standing order 38 each such motion is debatable.
That, I think, is the position under the rules. The Prime Minister has said that it is improper to suggest that there should be any debate on the merits of the resolution itself -that is, on the motion-because the house has already decided that such a resolution will be put forward in committee of the whole, and will there be discussed. But there is still necessary a formal motion that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair. That motion is exactly the same as the motion in connection with the consideration of a bill where, with Your Honour in the chair, the house has approved the principle of the bill. Then there is necessary still a further motion to be made by the minister who introduced the bill; and that is the motion that Mr. Speaker do leave the chair for the house to go into committee on the bill.
I do not claim to have done exhaustive research, but I have done some; and I find that that motion is debatable. The motion that Mr. Speaker leave the chair for the house to go into committee on the bill, even after we have just had second reading with Your Honour in the chair, is still debatable. And it is the same motion exactly as we now have before us-a motion for Your Honour to leave the chair for the house to go into committee on the resolution.
The authority which establishes that the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair on second reading of a bill is debatable is found at page 512 of the fourth edition of Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure. Bourinot is outlining the various stages gone through in dealing with a bill, and he comes to the stage of the order for a committee of the whole, and I quote from page 511 as follows:
When a bill has been read a second time by the clerk, the next question will be proposed:
"That the House go into committee on the bill (now, or on	next.)"
The house generally goes into committee on the bill at once-but when desired, the committee stage is postponed to another sitting of the house.
The motion generally passes, nem. con.-
A rough translation of that is "without opposition".
-like all such formal motions; though it is quite regular to move an amendment as to the time of committal.

Standing Order 60
When the order of the day for committee has been reached and called in due form the Speaker will put the question,
"That I do now leave the chair."
He puts that question: "On motion of Mr. So and So it is moved that I do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee on the said bill." Or, as we have it here, "that I do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee on the said resolution". He puts the question on the motion that he do now leave the chair. Bourinot continues:
Now is the time to move any amendment to this question. Members opposed to the bill may move that the house resolve itself into committee on the bill that day three or six months; or may propose motions adverse to the principle or policy of the measure.
That is, on the motion that the Speaker leave the chair. I submit that it is incontrovertible that that motion is exactly the same as the motion which we are now debating, for Your Honour to leave the chair for the house to go into committee on this resolution.
The reference which Bourinot gives to a case where such a motion was moved in the Canadian House of Commons was to an occasion back in 1875. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) will be interested in this. I quote from page 920 of Hansard of March 25, 1875, as follows:

I am not saying that it should happen; I am simply saying that our rules allow for it to happen just in the same way that I said we would not necessarily exercise our right every time to debate a resolution when the Speaker was in the chair, but we are arguing that we do have the right to do it when we consider the matter under discussion so important that it calls for such debate. That is all I am saying.

That concludes the third part of my argument. If the motion that the Speaker leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee after the second reading of a bill is debatable and is even capable of amendment-and precedents of this house establish that it is-then I submit that a motion that the Speaker leave the chair for the house to go into committee on a resolution is equally debatable and equally capable of amendment if hon. members wish to avail themselves of that right.
I conclude by coming back to the point with which I started, that the rules of the house were framed carefully to preserve the right to debate, to allow the opposition, which is a minority and which usually, although not always, represents a minority vote of the country, the right of full discussion. The rules were framed to protect the right to speak, so that there shall always be available for the benefit of the Canadian public full information, full opportunity for discussion of all measures'in the House of Commons so that the public may become fully informed as to the merits of the measure and so that the public's representatives in the house may become fully informed as to the intentions of the government with respect to the measure. And that is the particular purpose of rule 60 and rule 38, which in my submission permit debate on the resolution at this stage.

go into committee on the resolution is debatable. I submit that standing order 60 read together with standing order 38 establishes that fact and that the arguments I have put forward indicate how they do so. I conclude with the greatest deference-I know you will believe me when I say it is with the greatest deference-by saying that if I am right in that contention, that it is a rule of the house which permits debate, then debate can be precluded or taken awa^ only by a decision of the house to amend the rules. I contend that the rules of the house cannot be changed by a Speaker's ruling. The only thing which can take away the right to debate, if it exists, is a decision of this house.
Your Honour having said that you will be content to confine the debate to standing order 60, then we are faced with the simple proposition: Is the motion debatable or is it not debatable under that . rule? I submit that it is debatable and that it continues to be debatable until the House of Commons decides otherwise.

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) will allow me I wish to compliment him upon the most constructive contribution which he has made to this very debatable matter. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) spoke on this matter, I believe on February 17. Not having been trained either in the ministry or the law my remarks on this matter will not be as lengthy as those of the hon. members who have preceded me.
I think the question is this: Is the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair debatable at this stage of the resolution? There are various things that determine the procedure of this house. When there is no standing order or clearly defined regulation, custom and usage-that is, what has been done and what has been accepted-govern our procedure.
On that basis I think the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair to go into committee on the resolution is debatable. I would refer the house to citation 13 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition, which reads:
The proceedings of the houses (Senate and Commons) are governed by statutes, by rules and orders adopted by themselves, and by those usages which have grown up in the course of time and consequently become a part of their own practice or are derived from the common law of parliament by which they have consented to be guided in all matters of doubt. All "rules" are not "standing orders;" they may be sessional orders or merely precedents; but all "standing orders" are "rules".
Standing Order 60
Basing my argument first on that citation, may I say that I had already been in the house twelve years when the question came up in 1942 on which Mr. Speaker Glen made his decision as to the meaning of standing order 60. During those twelve years I cannot remember a question ever having arisen as to the right of members to have a debate on the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair at this stage of the resolution. Mr. R. B. Hanson, leader of the opposition at that time, I believe, said that in the twenty years prior to 1942 he never heard of the right being questioned. Therefore I think that usage has determined our right to speak on the resolution at this stage.
In my opinion the ruling that Mr. Speaker Glen made in 1942 was not logical, even if it were workable. He said that a debate was in order but that speakers could only speak on the negative side of the motion. I do not believe that you can have a debate when the debate is all on one side. I am quite convinced on that point and I do not believe that we should attempt to follow that ruling.
The arguments of those who say that there is no debate at this stage are based on standing order 60 which I should like to read again.
If any motion be made in the house for any public aid or charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof may not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned till such further day as the house thinks fit to appoint; and then it shall be referred to a committee of the whole house, before any resolution or vote of the house do pass thereupon.
I do not think it means that it shall be referred to committee of the whole without debate. In my opinion what this standing order deals with specifically is that no resolution or vote or financial commitment which will be a charge on the public treasury can be made while the Speaker is in the chair. That can be done only after the Speaker has left the chair and the house is in committee of the whole. I believe that is the central point of the standing order- "before any resolution or vote of the house do pass thereupon". In Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, when Dr. Beauchesne said this motion was debatable he was only putting in written form what already was the practice in the house.
Before I sit down I wish to point out one point that was raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). The ruling given by Mr. Speaker Glen was given on February 23, 1942, but on March 18, 1942, the then minister of finance (Mr. Ilsley) moved:

venture to make a few observations on 'the question we are now considering. What is it that we are considering? We are considering whether debate is allowable on the motion made by the responsible minister that the Speaker do now leave the chair.
That motion is made for the purpose of considering in committee a resolution standing in that minister's name. That resolution has to do with the expenditure of money and, theref ore, it can only be introduced by way of a resolution of the house. In that respect it is similar to a committee of supply. Now, if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) wished to make the motion that the Speaker do leave the chair for the purpose of resolving the house into committee of supply, then the considerations which are indicated in Durell's "Parliamentary Grants", 1917 edition, at page 25, would apply. There he says:
All proposals as to taxes or grants must in accordance with the rules ot procedure, be considered in the first place in committee of the whole house-
Then he says:
Such procedure which, as it has its foundation in prudence and an attention to the ease of the people ought to be in all instances invariably observed-
In the footnote the author refers back to 1667 when that principle was followed.
On the next page he says:
The demand for supplies having been made, the next step, therefore, is to refer it to the committee for consideration. But before the house can resolve itself into committee, the motion must be formally made and carried, 'that Mr. Speaker do leave the chair' since the Speaker does not preside over a committee of the house. It is the motion for this formality which1 illustrates and secures the ancient constitutional doctrine that the redress of grievances should precede supply; . . .
Now, sir, when you indicated that you wished this matter discussed in the house, I said to some of my colleagues who had more experience here than I have had: How is it that this house has been holding debates since 1867 and you are still in doubt about such a fundamental matter? If you cannot come
Standing Order 60
to a decision on precedents established in the past 85 or 86 years, why do you not go to the British house?
My hon. friend, the member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), said: They have altered their procedure over there and it is different from ours. I said: Let us then go back before they altered their procedure and see what the procedure was then-so I did that very thing although I had some difficulty locating it. Strange as it may seem, I did find a reference in Todd's "Parliamentary Government in England, 1869," volume 2, page 386. That reference was to a notice of motion introduced by Mr. Disraeli, who was prime minister and chancellor of the exchequer, on February 11, 1867, for submitting certain resolutions in connection with the reform bill of that time to the committee of the whole. He gave notice that he would, two weeks hence-and this was his notice of motion-on February 25, move that the house resolve itself into committee for the purpose of considering these resolutions.
So I went to Hansard and found that on the date in question, February 11, Mr. Disraeli had made a speech of over two hours and a half duration, and as a contrivance, to enable him to do that he spoke on one item from the speech from the throne. He gave notice then that on February 25 he would move that the house would resolve itself into committee on his resolutions. On February 25 he made a speech of an hour and a quarter to show why the house should resolve itself into committee.
All speeches made following Mr. Disraeli's were by the opposition and they were against the motion. There is nothing about the content of the resolutions because they were only bare resolutions such as we have before us now. It would be impossible to go into detail or a grand expose of what they involved, because they were just in skeleton outline. Several speakers from the opposition took part in the debate, but there was no other speaker from the government. The motion was withdrawn. It is a very interesting thing to note that it was on February 26 that third reading was given in the House of Lords to the British North America Act.
On February 26 the chancellor of the exchequer said he would withdraw his resolutions. Mr. Gladstone then spoke and said that if Mr. Disraeli had not done so he had intended to bring in an amendment to the motion that the Speaker do leave the chair.

What I want to say in that regard is that I went through a number of Hansards of the Canadian House of Commons taken at random. I found that from the earliest times down to recently when Mr. Mackenzie King was prime minister, and especially during the war, it was quite a common thing for a notice of motion to be given, that it is expedient for the house to go into committee to consider a certain resolution, and then on the motion that the Speaker do now leave the chair there would be a debate. I cannot say from memory if that debate was entirely confined to the negative, because it is some time since we had this matter before us. There is no doubt that there was a debate. It seems to me that the observation made by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) is incontrovertible. Here is an item on the order paper that the house go into committee on the resolution. I submit that under standing order No. 38 it is debatable without question. If you want to change that procedure, I 
suggest that you have to amend the rules. It cannot be done by any vote of the house. We may agree to dispense with any debate, but we cannot alter the rules without a substantive provision in that respect.

This difficulty arose, Mr. Speaker, for the first time on February 10 when Your Honour made a statement which is to be found at page 1784 of Hansard for that date. You said:
A matter has arisen as to what was said in the house on Friday. May I refer briefly to the debate which took place on that day. I have no hesitation in saying that, in view of that debate, I am quite concerned about the ruling I made in 1952 with respect to standing order 60.
Now, first of all, I should like to refer Your Honour to the key paragraph of your ruling in 1952. Then, I shall refer you to what did take place in the debate on that Friday to which you referred on February 10. The key paragraph of your ruling in 1952 will be found at page 3375 of Hansard for June 18, 1952. It reads as follows:
After giving this matter my careful consideration I have come to the conclusion that if there is no objection to the consideration of the resolution in committee of the whole, the motion that the Speaker do leave the chair should be put without debate. If any members are opposed to the resolution, and do not think that it should even be considered in the committee of the whole, or if they require additional information before agreeing to the motion, they should be given an opportunity to speak on the motion. The minister should endeavour to answer the objections which have been raised and to give the information requested.
Then, in the following paragraph, you went on to point out that you thought the practice of the minister opening the debate by a statement should be dropped. That was your very clear-cut ruling of June 18, 1952.
Then, I refer Your Honour to what happened in the debate on February 6. The debate was on a resolution preceding a bill to extend the Emergency Powers Act for a further year. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) was conducting the measure and he did not make a statement when the debate on the resolution stage commenced, thereby following the suggestion you had made in your ruling of 1952. Accordingly, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and several other members rose to state their objections to this measure going any further. They, too, were acting in accordance with your ruling of 1952. When they had finished, and when it appeared that the last speaker had made his objections, the Minister of Justice rose and, as found on page 1694 of Hansard for February 6, 1953, stated:
Mr. Speaker, if all those who wish to raise objections have done so, I believe it is my duty to answer the various objections, and I will be glad to endeavour to answer those that have already been made.

So far, he was following your ruling of 1952. Then, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) rose and said:
On a point of order, the minister does not presume by what he is saying to close the debate?

One of them is the suggestion by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) that the order made on this resolution, when it was originally introduced, is similar to the order that is made after the first reading of a bill. With that point I will deal just as a matter of fact, and I will call Your Honour's attention to the difference in form. When a bill receives first reading, it is then ordered for second reading at a future date; but there is no decision that it will be read a second time at a future date. It is ordered for second reading and that is the language you find in the Votes and Proceedings at page 366, for instance. That is the last one. Here is what we find:
Mr. Howe, seconded by Mr. Fournier (Hull), by leave of the house, introduced a bill, No. 233, an act to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, which was read the first time, and ordered for a second reading at the next sitting of the house.

The same language will be found in Votes and Proceedings at page 316. I will give Your Honour only three examples. At page 316 we find this language:
The following bills, from the Senate, were severally read the first time, on division, and ordered for a second reading at the next sitting of the house:
The same language-and it is the language that is used in all these cases-is used in the third example, at page 306 of Votes and Proceedings:
The following bills, from the Senate, were respectively read the first time and ordered for a second reading at the next sitting of the house:
I would ask you to contrast that language with the language used in Votes and Proceedings when this resolution came before the house for the second time and when it was resolved that at the next sitting the house would go into committee of the whole to consider the resolution as required by the terms of paragraph 360. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) referred to Beauchesne's third edition in which there is a statement that, on the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair for the house to go into committee to consider a resolution preceding a money bill, debate is allowed. As Your Honour pointed out, that was after Mr. Speaker Glen's ruling had been made to that effect and the Clerk of the House was reporting a ruling that had been made a few weeks before. You will find confirmation of that by referring to Beauchesne's second edition, page 347, part II of his rules and forms, paragraph (6), which was published before Mr. Glen's ruling and in which you find the following:
Moving Money Resolution:
Upon the following day,-
That is the day following the time when the house has resolved that it would at the next sitting go into committee of the whole to consider a resolution.
-or at such subsequent time as is convenient, when "government orders" are called, the minister may move the money resolution.

Mr. Chairman, the purpose of *this resolution is to seek authority to introduce a bill to revise and consolidate the Yukon Act. As the resolution states, it is also proposed to give legislative jurisdiction to the territorial council over certain matters which previously were dealt with by parliament. Under these headings are roads, wills, property of married women, coroners and inquests, controverted elections, the establishment and maintenance of hospitals, and agriculture.
The bill would also give authority to the commissioner in council to pass ordinances authorizing the commissioner, with the approval of the governor in council, to borrow money for purposes designated therein and to make loans to municipalities for the construction of municipal works.
Jurisdiction will also be sought to give the territorial council authority to increase the amount of the indemnity and living allowances of the members of the council and thus bring them more in line with those which may be paid to the elected members of the Northwest Territories.
Finally, the bill proposes to give the commissioner the right to hold lands for the beneficial use of the territory.
Apart from the changes I have mentioned, the bill will be a revision of the present act with a number of sections which are no longer necessary being dropped. The new act will be similar in many respects to the revised Northwest Territories Act which was enacted at the last session of parliament.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take advantage of this opportunity to bring to the attention of the house the very uncertain future of the farmers of Canada. I might say that in this connection I speak as a rancher with considerable experience and understanding, consequently I have a great deal of sympathy for the farmers in the uncertainty that faces them at this time.
I shall never forget nearly 50 years ago when we landed from a steamer on the Arrow lakes in British Columbia. The first two things from our effects that were put off that steamer were my father's silk top hat and a cross-cut saw. I always thought that was symbolic of the leisured past and the promised rigorous future. I shall never forget the trials of the people of those days in their efforts to clear the forest under great difficulty and to bring orchards into production.
I remember that my father was so anxious on one occasion to ship the first crate of cherries out of the district that he borrowed five pounds from a neighbour so he could fill up the crate. I mention this to indicate my intense sympathy for the farming population of this country and because there are hundreds of thousands of people throughout the country who have had similar experiences clearing land, building up farms and carrying on other activities in an effort to produce the food so necessary to our economy and to the people of this country.
With the approach of spring I consider this an appropriate time to bring this matter to the attention of the house and to ask for action by the government at this session along the lines we suggest. There is no question that during the last few months or perhaps the last year or so there has been a general decline in farm income across the country, while at the same time we have had increasing surpluses of some commodities, with increasing shortages in certain countries overseas whose populations exist at substandard levels. Not only has there been insecurity and instability created for the farming sections of our population, there has been instability of prices with a speculative element entering the picture so far as the consumer is concerned.
I have always thought that the farmer got, shall I say, the short end of the stick. It is generally recognized that the manufacturer has a recognized percentage of profit. The jobber selling agricultural commodities has a recognized percentage of profit. The wholesaler gets a recognized percentage of profit. The retailer gets a recognized percentage of profit. Position of Agricultural Industry must be met. What does the farmer get? He gets what is left when these people have taken their cuts. As I say, there are recognized fixed commissions and profits for these people, and guaranteed transportation charges.
Regardless of the repetition of the words "free enterprise" and "everyone for himself" I think it is quite fair to say that various sections of our economy have had their returns stabilized or more or less guaranteed only as a result of government action. Compare the position of corporations selling certain commodities to the dairy farmers, the fruit farmers, the poultrymen and all other agricultural producers, to that of the farmers. I noticed that three or four days ago Imperial Oil Limited of Vancouver and one or two other oil companies simply made an announcement in the press that the price of gasoline would increase by so many cents a gallon commencing on a certain date. They have control of their commodities, they have control of their prices, while the farmer is facing more and more insecurity under present conditions.
At the same time, as the result of legislation passed by this parliament and the provincial legislatures on which the processes of collective bargaining are based, organized labour has some stability of income for the life of the contracts which it signs with the companies for which its members are working and with which it is dealing. With spring approaching-and there is no question about it that hope springs eternal within the human breast-the farmer has no assurance of what he is going to receive for his crop when he harvests it next fall.
I am not going to speak at great length. I am just introducing the subject. In the monthly commercial letter of the Canadian Bank of Commerce for November there is a general review of agriculture which is well worth reading. Many of the monthly letters issued by our banks nowadays are well worth reading. They deal with the economic position of the country from an interesting point of view. The monthly letter of the Canadian Bank of Commerce to which I have referred has this to say about the agricultural industry:
The bulk of Canadian farm products is now marketed under some form of price support. This underwriting of farm prices has cushioned agriculture as a whole from the worst effects of the adverse conditions to which some branches have been subjected within the last year and a half, with the result that prices at the producers' level have declined only about 15 per cent . . .
There are one or two things I might point out in that connection. First of all this letter is published by a Canadian bank. I remember that when floor prices were suggested years ago some of the banking interests opposed the principle because they thought it was

Position of Agricultural Industry not a sound development in our economy. We see that today the principle of floor prices is recognized even by the banking institutions, and the good that has been done by the more or less minor application of the principle is recognized here. In addition, it is recognized that in the last year and a half farm prices have dropped about 15 per cent on the average, while we all know that the costs of production of the farmer have not declined to the same extent.
It is also very interesting to note that the banks of this country are showing more and more interest in the stability of Canadian agriculture. I remember when we faced a very difficult situation in the fruit industry of British Columbia in the mid-twenties, at a time when the growers were receiving far less than the cost of production. Previous to that there had been no organized assistance from the banks of the area, but even the banks were farsighted enough to see that if they were going to continue in business and make profits in that area they had to do something to assist in stabilizing that industry. When it came to reorganizing the fruit industry, building co-operatives and developing national marketing legislation, to the credit of the banks of the Okanagan and the Kootenays be it said that they got right behind the growers in their efforts to build some security for themselves in that field.
Not only do we find the banks concerned about the stability of agriculture; we also find that labour is getting more concerned. For years it was the current opinion of many labour and farming people that their interests were not identical but were opposed. That opinion has disappeared because everyone knows that the whole foundation of Canadian prosperity depends upon a sound agricultural economy. Therefore we find in various resolutions passed by labour organizations and in discussions at meetings, a growing consciousness on the part of organized labour that their prosperity is based to a great extent upon the prosperity of the farmer.
I do not happen to have at hand any quotations from Canadian labour publications that indicate that fact, but the same spirit is growing in the United States and to illustrate I am going to quote from the Manitoba Co-operator of March 19. The article is entitled "Straws in the Wind?" It reads in part as follows:
In its initial release this year, titled "The Meat of It," prepared and published by the research department, united packing house workers of America, C.I.O., Chicago, the union publication under a heading "A Depression for Agriculture?" notes with concern the decline in the net income and purchasing power of the farmer in the United States. A chart to show the general downward
[Mr. Herridge.l

trend since 1947 is included and is supplemented by the following paragraphs-
I think these paragraphs are most interesting.
"There are many things one could say about the increasingly dark farm picture, for it has become darker since this chart was prepared. But we can sum it up by recalling that the symptoms of a 'sick agriculture' were becoming increasingly acute during the 'prosperous twenties,' noting that today's symptoms are disturbingly like those of that earliest period, and warning that history could repeat itself.
The feature about that history to remember is not the crashing stock market, the closed banks or even the recently rich men jumping out of windows. Instead it is that the sickness of U.S. agriculture was one of the main sources of infection which caused a prolonged and devastating illness for the entire economy.
Have we learned enough since that earlier malady? If so, we won't be content to let 'nature take its course' in solving the price and income problems of our farming population. We won't be satisfied either by the appointment of advisory or investigating commissions most of whose members, no matter how much they may know about certain aspects of agriculture, are also members of big corporate boards of directors."
Then the article continues:
Because the trend of farm income and purchasing power in Canada somewhat parallels that of the United States, the deliberations of the conference will be awaited with deep interest.
It is because we in this group do not believe in a return to the conditions of the mid or late twenties and do not believe in allowing nature to take its course in the marketing of farm products that we are bringing this question before the house at this appropriate time. In addition, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture made representations to the government quite recently. The farmers met the cabinet on March 6, 1953 and made their usual excellent annual representations. In a paragraph dealing with price fluctuations and price support I read the following:
Surplus production and low prices for a farm product inevitably result in scarcity and high prices at a later date. Such extreme flexibility could be reduced if the policy of the agricultural prices support board were administered, not as a stock loss device only as at present-
That, Mr. Speaker, is the biggest complaint of this group.
-but rather as a device for preventing wide swings in production and price. Such a change in emphasis would in some cases mean a more generous application of the price floor principle than has been the case in the past.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we do not for a moment underestimate the value this legislation has been to the farmers of this country. We give the government credit for introducing it, but what we are seeking is the fuller use of the legislation to provide the greatest stability for agriculture in this country.

Instability is being felt by the poultry producers, the dairymen, the meat producers, the wheat producers and by all sections of agriculture. I am sure, from the activities of farm organizations from their briefs, from the press and from the correspondence I have received that there is in the minds of the farmers of this country at this time a greater sense of insecurity than has existed for some years.
As I said before, we believe that farm prosperity is essential for a healthy Canadian economy. With a world food shortage we believe that production must be maintained. At this point I wish to bring out the fact that we repeatedly hear our country and our way of life referred to as a Christian civilization. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, it is complete humbug and hypocrisy to consider ours a Christian civilization if we do anything to restrict agricultural production while there are hundreds of millions of people in the world today who are short of food.
Mr. Speaker, we are in a happy position in Canada to do something about this. We have the act on the statute, and it has functioned to a moderate degree and with some advantage to the farmers of Canada. In addition we have a perfect set-up for our government to take action in a democratic way. We have our large farm organizations representing various groups, the machinery is all established, and they are willing to co-operate with the government to do something along the lines I am suggesting this afternoon.
I am quite sure, Mr. Speaker, that our proposals will be supported by speakers from other groups in this house this afternoon. As I said before, the legislation is sound in principle but we are seeking amendments that will provide for a fuller use of the act as the result of co-operation on the part of the government with the producers' organizations, and a formula being included in the act that will provide the producers with returns in relation to the general standards of the time. Surely that is not too much to ask, that the basic primary producers of this country be given the modest security that can be given them under the terms of this legislation.
Mr. Speaker, I have more or less dealt in generalities, but before I can conclude I do want to say a word or two about the fruit industry. As I said before, the government has the machinery at hand to work out a very fair and effective policy to provide some stability for the farmers of this country at the present time. It is the general policy of the British Columbia fruit growers' association to discuss their problems with members
Position of Agricultural Industry of the Canadian horticultural council, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the provincial and federal governments. I know the minister is fully aware of the problems which face the fruit industry in this country, in the maritimes, Ontario and British Columbia. I see the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) listening with great interest, and I am very ipleased on that account. I will say now, in fairness to the minister, that I happen to know that he is using his best efforts to assist the British Columbia fruit industry.
Last year the total apple production in North America was such that it offered few problems. On the whole the growers received reasonable returns. The soft fruit industry, however, experienced a very poor year for two reasons. First, there was a very heavy crop in both the United States and Canada; and second-a more or less artificial condition-there was a change in the relationship between Canadian and United States dollars. I know some producers are inclined to suggest that the remedy for this situation is higher tariffs. However, because of our general approach to this economic problem, our obligations to the United Nations, and the necessity for freeing world trade, we believe that we must find some other solution to produce some stability in this branch of agriculture.
I mentioned a moment ago that our tree fruit industry in British Columbia practises co-operation with other groups in the industry, with the provincial government and with the federal government. To illustrate that I wish to read one paragraph of a report by Mr. A. E. Garrish, president of the British Columbia fruit growers' association, to the last annual convention. This is what he has to say:
It might be in order at this time to mention that we, in the tree fruit area of British Columbia, are part of a very large industry which has grown to its present size slowly and painfully over a long period of time. What progress has been achieved has been through a process of discussion and compromise inspired by good will and a desire to co-operate. We, in our association, have learned to think in terms of our industry rather than in terms of local, or sectional, interests. It is equally important that in our representation on the national level we be prepared to see the whole picture and not just our side of it and that our presentations at ail times be sound, constructive and moderate, so that we may maintain the standing which has been built up.
While we endeavour to solve our problems to the best of our ability, some problems can be solved only by government action and must be kept constantly in front of the responsible officials. This can best be done by co-ordinating our approach to the government with that of other fruit producing areas through the medium of the Canadian Horticultural Council.

Position of Agricultural Industry
That is the attitude, Mr. Speaker, of the tree fruit industry in British Columbia and, I think it is the attitude of agricultural organizations generally. That is the reason I say there is a wonderful opportunity, with the legislation we have on the books at the present time and with the agricultural organizations we have in the country, to do something sound and fundamental to produce some stability for agriculture. I mention the soft fruit industry particularly because of its difficulties last year and owing to the fact that I have peach growers, prune growers and other soft fruit growers in my constituency. I know they will welcome the fact that I have mentioned their difficulties to the house and that the problem has the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and our energetic Minister of Fisheries.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that, in view of the soft fruit growers' difficulties being caused by the action of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) the government has in this case particular responsibility for measures to remove this injustice. Therefore I suggest that first of all consideration be given to a floor price being established for soft fruit this year, as a result of consultation with the industry. I also suggest that the government, in co-operation with the industry, make every effort to increase markets for tree fruits at home and abroad.
I would say that while the farmers of this country are facing an uncertain future there is a necessity for the greater use of funds under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, at a time when considerable relief from taxation has been given to the large corporations of this country. I am of the opinion that at least some of the relief, some of the savings that have been handed to the large corporations of this country, could have been used by this government to support the agricultural industry to the greater advantage of the economy as a whole.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as I said before, we have instability and insecurity. I know that, in addition to the fruit industry of British Columbia, we have instability and insecurity in so far as the poultry producers are concerned. We are in a very fortunate marketing area, but costs have been such and prices have been such that only the most efficient have been able to survive during the last two or three years. This situation can only be remedied as a result of government action. Producers' organizations in all sections of agriculture are helping themselves to the limit of their ability, but they can only go so far. If we are going to do something for them, they

must have government assistance and government co-operation. I suggest, therefore, that now is the time for the government to give consideration to this need for stability, and to the amendments to the act that will provide that necessary stability following government action.
I am only speaking about general principles. As I said before, others will deal with the details of this situation that I have overlooked or omitted. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones):
