I take this opportunity of bringing forward a number of matters in connection with the agricultural situation. This motion enables members of the house to place before the house matters of importance to different segments of the community. I intend to say a few words particularly along the lines of the amendment just ruled out of order by Your Honour, because I think the time has come for a discussion of this subject in the house. What I intend to do in general is to refer to one or two matters upon which there has been no discussion during this session, with a view to ascertaining the position of affairs, and in particular to the fear of Canadian farmers regarding sliding prices and lost markets.
I realize that during 1952 there was a pronounced increase in the production of farm products in Canada, but it will have been noted that during that year, while there was a material increase in the quantity of production, there was not an increase in the amount paid to Canadian farmers. I am going to refer to one or two suggestions to which I made reference a few days ago in a speech outside the house. I want to point out particularly that, while in 1952 there was a very much larger production of farm products in Canada, the value in that year was $2,787,800,000 which was $38 million below the all-time high of 1951. In other words, while in 1952 production went up by approximately 12 per cent, there was a reduced return to the farmer and there was also an increase in the cost of the things purchased by the farmer of approximately 5 per cent.
I think that generally speaking today across this country farmers are worried
23, 1953
Position of Agricultural Industry about conditions. In the present situation they do not yet see, nor do I, the ingredients of 1928 or 1929; but they do fear that unless action is taken by parliament now, with the loss of farm markets-however the government may say that it has not lost any markets-the situation is fraught with danger.
I mentioned a moment ago that they fear the situation generally. They also wonder why parliament is not taking some action. In a recent representation made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture the whole situation was summed up in these words: While Canada today is undoubtedly enjoying an era of extraordinary prosperity, agricultural producers, particularly in the field of livestock and livestock products, find themselves victims of an economic squeeze between declining farm returns and rising farm costs.
That situation applies rather generally all along the line, and it is causing a serious fear to be aroused in the minds of farmers in general. I believe their request to parliament is that a full discussion on the subject take place now, and that action be taken immediately in order to forestall the possibility of a deteriorating price level and a loss of markets which, in 1928 and 1929, led finally to a depression.
As was said by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, regardless of what prosperity there may be in other industries, and regardless of the tremendous increases that are taking place in mineral production in this country, in large measure owing to the demands of war or the preparations for the assurance of peace, nonetheless, unless agriculture is prosperous, that prosperity created in that way cannot but be short-lived; for those mineral products are in fact exhaustible and are being exhausted whereas agricultural products are produced continuously and repeatedly from year to year.
What I intend to do on this occasion is to refer but briefly to the general situation, because parliament as yet is completely in the dark as to what is happening at Washington. We in parliament learn what is happening at Washington at the international wheat conference not in parliament-because we are denied information here-but through the medium of the press. That is the only way we are able to secure any information. During recent days and weeks, on more than one occasion the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has been asked: What is the situation? What is being done? What stand is being taken by the representatives of Canada with respect to negotiations leading to another international wheat agreement? Yet up until this moment parliament

Position of Agricultural Industry has been vouchsafed no information whatsoever. Today the Canadian Press carried an article to the following effect:
Prolonged Washington negotiations on a new international wheat agreement will be continued for another week in a last-ditch effort to break a price deadlock, informants said Saturday.
Exporters are still holding out for a ceiling of $2.10 a bushel, while importers, with Britain at the lead, have refused to go any higher than $1.95.
However, the 42 importing countries are expected to hold another meeting next Tuesday-
That is tomorrow.
-at which time Britain likely will suggest that the offer be increased to $2 a bushel.
With increasing farm costs, a price level such as that suggested in today's Canadian Press article will, I think, be most detrimental to the wheat producer of this country on the basis of the suggested maximum and minimum prices set forth in that article; and it is borne out by a similar article in the New York Times. The western wheat farmer will find himself in a position that cannot but cause worry and concern. I cannot understand why parliament cannot secure any information on a matter that affects the livelihood of hundreds of thousands of people within this country. It is a matter that deserves consideration and that ought to have had consideration long ago, but it is one which parliament has had no opportunity to discuss in order to place before the government and the country the views of farmers in general.
I think we should be entitled to some information. During the last several years the international wheat agreement has been in effect, farm costs have been rising. On more than one occasion I asked whether or not the Minister of Trade and Commerce would give consideration to asking the purchasing countries to accept some escalator clause whereby, in the event of increasing farm costs, there would be increases in the minimum price, but the answer generally given was that nothing was going to be done about it. Indeed, the minister refused to discuss the matter at all.
I believe that, in the matter of our defences, the countries who are today in the main the buying countries should realize that if our wheat economy does not secure a fair return, Canada's agricultural plant for the production of wheat and wheat products- which are so necessary to our defence and that of the other NATO countries-would be seriously affected. We are in a position where, if communism marches, the only NATO countries whose production of wheat and other farm products will not immediately be seriously affected, if not entirely obliterated, will be the United States of America

and Canada. In the interests of our cooperative defence with the other members of NATO, I believe that Canada's productive machine should be maintained and sustained at a high level in order to meet the eventuality of war should it ever take place.
In the second place I believe there should be a realization by those countries that in a common prosperity, and in the preservation of this productive machine for wheat, the greatest hope for the future exists against communism. It should also be realized at this time that as between nations, members of NATO, quotas and restrictions against farm products should not be considered, much less imposed. The action taken in 1951 by the United States government in prohibiting the import of certain Canadian dairy products has had an extremely serious effect on Canada's dairy industry. It cannot be justified in the world of today. Objection was taken to that action by the government in a message delivered in February. But for some reason the United States government has not seen fit to remove the quota system or the embargo. The result is that surpluses of cheese and other dairy products are mounting, and the situation therefore is that, even in the world of today which demands far greater agricultural production than at present prevails, with mounting surpluses farm prices will necessarily fall, and fall out of proportion with other prices.
Certainly a successful farm production plant will never be maintained in Canada if the farmer is in the paradoxical position of being in a world where there must be farm production in order to feed hungry people everywhere and thus prevent their becoming a fertile recruiting ground for communism, while at the same time if the farmers do produce surpluses, the farm production plant of Canada is in danger of being undermined, if not destroyed.
Certainly during the early twenties the tariff imposed by the United States against Canadian farm products had an effect which, in the later twenties, culminated in an almost complete destruction not only of the Canadian farm production plant but also, because of low prices, of the will on the part of Canadian farmers to produce.
In a speech delivered during the election campaign in 1945 the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) pointed out that one of the main reasons for the fall in the prices of farm products in the thirties was the action taken by the United States of America. I think the time has come for the government of Canada to point out in the strongest possible terms to the United States government that its action in 1951 in regard

to dairy products seriously militates against this country doing its full share in the preservation of the agricultural production plant which, once destroyed, would take years to restore.
In that connection I feel the protest made in February was couched in more diplomatic language than it would have been if the farmers of Canada had had anything to do with the preparation of that message.
In so far as wheat production is concerned,
I feel the farmers should have some assurance as to what is being done in Washington. Certainly it is going to have a very serious effect if this conference, which first took place in London and, failing to arrive at an agreement, adjourned to Washington, falls to pieces, and this at a time when wheat production is so necessary, despite the fact that at the moment we have an unsold surplus amounting to about 650 million bushels. Markets have been or will be found for part of that amount.
So far as our market in Great Britain for other food products is concerned, one has only to read the Economic Record, a publication issued by the United Kingdom information office, to realize that today Great Britain would be purchasing many farm products that are surplus in this country if arrangements could be made either to make currency convertible or to allow Great Britain to supply us with tens of millions of dollars worth of defence products with which she could supply us. A credit would be secured for Great Britain, thus enabling her to purchase our farm products in surplus supply.
Many interesting facts are set out in this issue of the Economic Record for February of this year. It states that the $1,500,000 required to purchase about 5 million tons of cheddar cheese from Canada was found only because of unexpected dollar payments by Canada to the United Kingdom under the Canada-United Kingdom-New Zealand meat agreement.
Well, if credits could be arranged in that connection and to that extent to take care of that portion of the surplus in cheese, could not the same have been done in greater measure through the purchase of defence requirements Canada needs, and which Great Britain is able to produce, so as to assure that this market can be kept open for us? For, talk as some will, while the United States market is contiguous to us, and comfortably situated, and while it would be economical if it was always open to us, history has shown clearly that whenever we have had farm surpluses the United States has been in much the same position. Then the Economic Record goes on to say:
The United Kingdom market absorbs about 20 per cent of total world exports of bacon and ham and before the war people in Britain ate 600,000 tons, of which about one third was home produced . . . Britain has not been able to find the dollars to buy bacon from Canada where, before the war, some 68,000 tons were obtained and 95,000 tons (by no means a record high) in 1948.
May I repeat the suggestion I made a moment ago, that I do not believe the Department of Defence Production has gone far enough in the way of encouraging the purchase in Great Britain of those things that can be produced there, and which are required for defence.
Then this publication deals with meat, and points out that Great Britain today is buying more and more from Australia under longterm agreements, and also under the recent Anglo-Argentinian agreement, under which 238,000 long tons of carcass meat will be supplied this year. It states that this is an improvement over the 1952 imports from the Argentine. I realize reference will be made to prices paid under that agreement. But the fact remains that, however much members of the government may deny it, we have indeed lost our market in Great Britain for many of our agricultural products, and that market will not be restored to us unless serious steps are taken in connection with obtaining many of our defence requirements from Great Britain, thus creating a credit in funds which will preserve the market for farm products of this country. At the rate at which markets have disappeared, regardless of any increase in Canadian consumption because of a rising standard of living, we are going to find ourselves faced with undisposed-of surpluses; and the degree to which such surpluses will affect the economy, aside from the prosperity of the farmer, is shown in the supplementary estimates, where over $30 million is to be voted to pay for the maintenance of certain floor prices.
I feel that the subject of floor prices is one that should be discussed, and the time is ripe for the discussion of that question. Therefore I feel that an amendment would be in order at this time to give the house an opportunity of voting on the question. I believe that Canadian farmers are asking for fair farm price levels that bear some relationship to the prices of the products the farmer has to purchase. Therefore I intend to move an amendment very similar to the

Position of Agricultural Industry one this party has moved on previous occasions, and which I drafted following the disposition of the one just moved. I move, seconded by Mr. Ross (Souris):
That all the words alter "that" to the end of the question be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to provide floor prices for agricultural products at such levels as to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship.
Unfortunately I have not extra copies of the amendment, but it does represent the desire and I believe the demand on the part of Canadian farmers in general that action be taken now, before Canada finds itself in the position of having surplus production. We realize the needs of the NATO countries for all-out production in order to meet the eventuality that peace should cease to exist; and in order to maintain, farmers on the farms something must be done to remove the squeeze that is taking place because of falling prices which have resulted, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, in a reduction in income of 12 per cent in 1952 over 1951, while the production of agricultural products was materially increased during the same period and farm costs have risen by 5 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, for the third time this afternoon

I regret that it has again become necessary for me to plead for equitable prices for the products of the agricultural industry. On different occasions during the present and previous sessions many of us have insisted that something should be done, yet this afternoon we find the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) trying to find some flaw in the amendment just presented. I hope that before this debate finishes he will have something more constructive to give to the agricultural industry than the excuse he offered just a moment ago.
We all realize that agriculture is the backbone of this country. Perhaps that cannot be said of some other countries, but we can continue to make that statement without fear of successful contradiction as far as Canada is concerned. The prosperity of many groups in Canada depends upon the prosperity of agriculture. Therefore I feel it is the duty of all sections of this house to see to it that agriculture gets a square deal.
They have an agricultural industry in the United States, and that government seems to do something about conditions when they get down to a certain level. The Alberta Wheat Pool Budget of February 27 contains an article from the XJ.S. News and World Report entitled "Farmers Being Squeezed" which reads:
As things size up, the outlook for business suggests this:
Peak in activity is passing. Farmers are hurt. Businessmen in farm communities find business slower. Exporters, generally, are hurt too. There's no zip left in any big line of business, though activity is high.
More lines will begin to slip as 1953 wears on. Builders face problems. Manufacturers, in many fields, will find goods harder to move. Dealers, merchants often are likely to be complaining about demand. A turn from years of inflation to mild deflation is to make its appearance.
Trends, barring bigger war, will be gradually downward. Jobs, probably, will be less abundant. Prices, often, will be tending down. The boom, quite definitely, will be over. Adjustment will be under way.
That's the way it appears from the signs that are gathering.
Farmers, even with government help, are in a squeeze right now.
A farmer, on the average, in 1953, will get a smaller proportion of the national income than in any years since the depression bottom in 1932.
He will have many more dollars than in 1932, but relative to other parts of the population, his share of the total will be back at a low level. Put it this way:	One person out of six in the country
is a farmer. In 1946, when times were best for farmers, $1 out of $9 in national income went to the farmer. In 1953, $1 in $15 will go to the farmer. Farmers, relative to other groups, are slipping. There's political trouble for Eisenhower in that simple fact. There also is to be a test of the theory that people are willing to forgo constant doses of government inspired inflation, even if times get a little harder.

We find that there is something of interest to our Canadian farmers in the treatment of United States farmers. It will be of great interest to note the statement made by President Eisenhower, and I quote from the overseas report on agricultural developments, economics division, marketing service, Department of Agriculture, which contains the following on page 4:
Some changes, perhaps of a substantial and fundamental nature, may be made in agricultural policies by the new Republican administration. In his state of the union message to Congress on February 2, President Eisenhower referred to the slow, irregular decline in farm prices which has been going on for two years, and promised that prices of basic commodities will be supported at 90 per cent of parity until the end of 1954 . . . We should begin now to consider what farm legislation we should develop for 1955 and beyond. Our aims should be economic stability and full parity of income for American farmers.
What is happening in Canada? From time to time we hear many speeches made, but speeches alone will not improve the condition of our farmers. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) went to London a few months ago to take part in the prime ministers' conference. We expected then that many of the obstacles to freer trade would be removed, but up to the present time not many results have been obtained. Recently we have had statements by Henry Ford, Jr., in connection with removing obstacles to freer trade. The president of the Ford Motor Company of Canada, Mr. Sale, also made a statement which I read into the record on February 26 last. The Minister of Finance agreed with the statement made by Mr. Sale, but when he delivered his budget speech on February 19 he apologized that he was making very few changes in the tariff.
That is the help our farmers are getting. So far as the farming industry is concerned, concessions were made on plow bolts and a few minor farm implements. I do not think that is the way to help agriculture. At the present time agriculture should be helped in every way possible because many people tell us that the best way to defeat communism is to feed the people in those countries that are threatened by it, and in those countries that already have had communism inflicted upon them. But we do not see very much being done to help. Prices are slipping in the agricultural industry and costs are increasing. According to information we have, costs increased in 1952 by 7 per cent; but if we take the prices of several commodities being produced by farmers we find that they have gone down, and it does not seem that very much is being done to increase them.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I had been discussing the question of agriculture in the United States and Canada, and had referred to statements made by some of the political and industrial leaders of Canada. I feel that while many speeches and statements have been made there are different methods that could be adopted to assist agriculture and, by so doing, assist the economy of the whole country. I think it is about time we started in to do some of those things.
One of the things we could do would be to keep production costs down. On many occasions I have referred to the excessive cost of farm implements. I notice that some of the implement companies claim that their prices have not increased very much, but only a few days ago I received some information from the dominion bureau of statistics which I might give the house. The figures are based on an index price for farm machinery for 1935-39 equalling 100.
In 1948 machinery prices stood at 141-6. In 1949 the index increased to 158-3. In 1950 there was another increase to 165-1. In 1951 the index jumped to 186-8 and in 1952 it jumped again to 195-4. That represents an increase of approximately 54 points in the price index of farm machinery in five years. I think it is time, when the machinery companies do not themselves do something, for the government to act and see that farmers are not soaked in this way.
In the Ottawa Citizen of Tuesday, November 25, 1952, under the heading "Report farm machinery parts dumped" I find something that may be of interest. Under a Winnipeg dateline it says:
Customs officials in Winnipeg are reported investigating complaints that castings for agricultural machinery are being dumped here by American firms south of Minneapolis at as much as 50 per cent below the Manitoba price.
The castings are for seeders, disc plows and other farm equipment.
Customs officials said there was normally no tax on such farm equipment from the United States, but, if dumping could be proved, a dumping duty, raising the price to fair market value, would be imposed and would be paid by the importer.
I think that is further evidence to show that we are paying much more in Canada for our implements and parts than we should pay. In the United States they pay higher wages than we do, they get much of their raw material from Canada, and there is no reason we should pay such high prices. Again I say, why not investigate the price of farm implements.

Position of Agricultural Industry We have still another .load placed on the backs of farmers through increased freight rates. Recently in this house a return was brought down in my name showing increases in freight rates in the past five years. The first increase was 21 per cent and it meant an additional $282 million in freight rates. The next increase was 20 per cent which, on the cumulative tariff, amounted to 45-2 per cent and an additional $197,400,000. The next freight rate increase was 17 per cent, which raised the cumulative total to 69-9 per cent, and accounted for an additional $86,700,000. Those three increases amounted to a .total of $566,100,000. There is another increase of 9 per cent pending, and it will run the total over the last five years up to 85-2 per cent. The weight of this freight rate charge is borne either directly or indirectly by the farmer, mainly in western
Canada because that is where we have most of our production.
We have to pay freight eastward on our grain, and on many of the things we purchase we also have to pay the freight westward. Every time the railways take a notion that they should have another freight rate increase they make the necessary application and invariably it is granted. I think some further consideration should be given before any more freight rate increases are granted to the railways. There are other methods by which they can keep within their budgets.
We have been told that Canada's agricultural industry is in a very prosperous condition. I do not entirely agree with that statement, because when we analyse some of the conditions which exist today we find that the picture will not bear it out. Some of the reasons for the apparent prosperity in Canada might be summed up as follows. First, we had heavy grain crops in 1951 and 1952. Prices, of course, have not been climbing; they have been falling, and that has something to do with our not getting better returns from our grain. The crop in 1952, I might say, was the best we have ever had in western Canada, and the resulting prosperity is reflected all over Canada. Again, we had good prices for beef but those prices, I am sorry to say, have slipped. They have skidded; and apparently that skidding has not yet stopped. We had fairly good floor prices for hogs but farmers in all provinces of Canada are not satisfied that the prospects are good for raising hogs in 1953 because, in all provinces except the one from which I come, Alberta, the production of hogs has decreased. I do not know but I believe that help in the form of floor prices will be required to bolster prices of that commodity.
In my opinion the future for agriculture is not as bright as it might be. I see that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is in his seat so I will say that I believe his intentions are good, but I do not think his colleagues in the cabinet have yet learned the importance of agriculture in this country.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has lived in Saskatchewan for a number of years, and he has had a picture of agriculture in that particular area. Apparently he has not been able to convince his colleagues that certain things should be done. I know he has been trying, but if he has not been successful then perhaps other members of the house may be able to give him some assistance. At a meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in Montreal a little over a year ago the minister, in effect, told that gathering that they should not increase production of certain farm products. I believe that was
Position of Agricultural Industry sound advice because he realized, as many of us did, that there was no market for increased production. In case anyone should get false ideas about conditions today, all they have to do is read the speech the Minister of Agriculture made a short time ago to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in Victoria in which, according to newspaper reports, he told the farmers that they should cut down production in order to keep prices at a remunerative level.
With conditions as they are, as I pointed out before; with millions of people in this world going to bed hungry every night, I think a policy of that sort is criminal and should not be allowed to exist. By supporting reasonable and equitable floor prices for our products, at perhaps a smaller cost to the country than most of us imagine, we could increase our production. The president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, Mr. Hannam, feels the same way the minister does about this problem. I think it is about time those in responsible positions on the government benches took this problem to heart and did something realistic about it.
The minister does not seem to like the word "parity". I do not know why he has a distaste for it, but he does not seem to like it. Some short time ago he told us that in place of parity the government would see to it that the farmers got prices comparable to those which were received in the years 1943, 1944 and 1945. According to the figures from the bureau of statistics, we find that the prices paid do not measure up to that promise. Even though we have floor prices provided which do not measure up to the prices which existed in the periods mentioned, they are mainly for the protection of the packers and the producers do not get much benefit at the point of delivery.
On March 5 the Minister of Agriculture made another speech. I am surprised that he made it, because he must not expect many people are gullible enough to swallow the statements he made. He compared the six years after the war with the six years before the war, and that certainly was not fair. He realizes, just as all of us here do, that the six years before the war were still in the depths of the depression. So far as the wheat grower of western Canada is concerned, he stayed in that depression until August, 1943. I believe that is the time our initial price was raised above 70 cents per bushel. Before that time we had heavy taxation levied, and we are still groaning under that burden. The six years after the war were years of prosperity brought about by the war and by preparations for, and the fighting of, the present

Position of Agricultural Industry undeclared war. It is a war, even though it is not declared. The fellows who are over there in the trenches, suffering through snowstorms and other hardships, realize that it is a war. We should recognize that and treat those people accordingly.
Up to the present there has -been no attempt to devise any effective remedy. That is a mistake, because it is affecting the whole economy of our country. According to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) 1951 was the best year we have had, and at that time nearly 25 per cent of the population of Canada was on the land. In that year this 25 per cent received only 9 [DOT] 95 per cent of the national income. I ask the government whether that is a fair percentage of the national income for the farmers to receive. These people work, in some seasons of the year, not 8 hours a day but 16 hours, and in some cases more than that because help is not to be had. In 1952 we had over 20 per cent of the population on the land, and those people received only a little over 13 per cent of the national income. There must be some reason for the reduction in the population on the land, and I believe that is because in other lines of industry there are better pay, better working conditions, pensions and so forth. The result is that we have not the farm population which a country like Canada could support if we had proper agricultural policies laid down and administered.
Before the dinner recess I was dealing to some extent with agricultural prices in the United States. In the Western Producer of September 24 last, under the heading "Support price set at $2.21 a bushel for 1953 United States wheat crop," I find this:
A national average support price of not less than $2.21 a bushel for the 1953 United States wheat crop was announced last week by secretary of agriculture Charles F. Brannan.
This is 90 per cent of the August, 1952, wheat parity price of $2.46. Support for the 1952 crop wheat, now eligible for loan and purchase agreement, is a national average of $2.20 a bushel.
A minimum price support is announced at this time in accordance with the ''forward pricing" provisions of the Agricultural Act of 1949. If the wheat parity price as of July 1, 1953, is higher, the support level will be increased to reflect 90 per cent of the wheat parity price at that time. In no event will the support be lower than the $2.21 national average announced.
The 1953 crop wheat will be supported through farm storage and warehouse storage loans and by the offer of the Commodity Credit Corporation to purchase wheat delivered by producers under purchase agreements. Loans and purchase agreements will be available from time of harvest through January 31, 1952. The loans will mature April 30, 1954, or earlier on demand.
At the time the election campaign in the United States was being waged many people were worried about agricultural policy if a

new administration were elected. Since the election, however, President Eisenhower has stated that they will continue the present parity price program until 1954, when they will carry not only 90 per cent of parity but will increase that to 100 per cent. I think that Canada could take a leaf out of the book of the government of the United States in that connection.
At the present time we have the wheat importing and exporting countries meeting in Washington to consider the signing of a new international wheat agreement. Only this morning I read that the exporters want $2.10 a bushel, while the importers are only prepared to pay $1.95. We do not know what the outcome of that struggle will be. So far as this group is concerned, we favour an international wheat agreement. We do not, however, favour sacrificing price in order to have an agreement. We must have a price that will give our wheat producers enough to cover the cost of production and something besides, because all other groups in the country are getting that.
If the wheat agreement should not be completed, I feel that we must continue the Canadian wheat board in operation. Regardless of whether or not the agreement is signed, the wheat board must not be allowed to go out of business because, in my opinion, that board is the last hope of the farmers.
We in this group feel that we should have parity prices for agricultural products. If the crumbling set-up that we have today will not provide them-and 1 think two or three years ago in London the Minister of Agriculture made some extremely critical remarks about those controlling our money system-there is another method that will provide parity prices, just prices, for all the commodities we can produce here. By providing them, we can provide not only for our agriculturists but for all in Canada the best that it is possible for the country to produce, and let them enjoy it in peace and without having to fight wars in order to bring us out of slumps, as we have seen on three different occasions since I came to this country less than forty years ago.

Mr. Speaker, there is one thing I wish to touch on and that is the question of the sale of our wheat. The farmers in western Canada, long before I had any interest in farming, were looking for stable wheat prices. We came out of the first great war with rather high wheat prices, and we enjoyed an era of prosperity. Then during the early twenties they declined, and in the late twenties we had good wheat marketing again. Then in the early thirties we had a carryover of millions of bushels of wheat-I would say hundreds of millions of

bushels-in this country which we could not sell at any price. That situation was cured to some extent by the second war when a goodly number of countries were out of production, and we did see a gradual rise in the world wheat market.
Then after the second world war we started to market in bulk. A goodly number of the countries of the world felt that bulk wheat marketing was the way they wanted to do their wheat marketing; and we accommodated the world market by instituting a system of bulk marketing here. The farmers and the farm organizations with whom I have been acquainted feel that, as far as they are concerned, we in this country should continue a system of bulk wheat marketing through the board.
When the Saskatchewan wheat pool and the other pools were formed, the chief reason for their existence was that the farmers wanted a steady, stable price for wheat at any time they wished to deliver it. The reason they desired that condition was this. When the average farmer gets ready to pay his year's bills in the fall, his wheat is forced on the market; he has to sell it. World wheat buyers know that when there is a forced sale, the price will naturally be low. Then during the spring, when the farmer had no more wheat left to sell, the price of wheat goes up. The relatively high market that might prevail in the spring was never available to the average farmer because he sold his wheat at a low price in the fall.
As we got into the period of world war II and set up the Canadian wheat board, we got an entirely new conception. We had the wheat pools trying to do this before. The Saskatchewan wheat pool got into a great deal of trouble in trying to finance the Saskatchewan crop. Then during the war, with the Canadian wheat board we got into a position where the Dominion of Canada was prepared to finance the wheat crop, and that was much more satisfactory to the farmers than the condition we had had before. We sold wheat, millions and millions of bushels of it, on the world wheat market at a fair high price.
In Saskatchewan and in western Canada as a whole, if we want to exist we have to sell a large volume of wheat. Wheat is the best commodity for us to produce. It is durable; it is easy to handle; it is cheap to ship, and it is the ideal commodity for us to grow. We should continue to stress that volume is the main thing we are after in the handling of this foodstuff.
We in western Canada normally grow some 350 million bushels of wheat every year. In 1952 we grew some 600 million
Position of Agricultural Industry bushels of wheat. At the present time the amount in store in the world is as follows. In Canada we have some 550 million bushels of wheat. In the United States they have nearly 750 million bushels. In Australia and the Argentine they have another few hundred million bushels. This makes a total on the world market at the present time of something over 1,400 million bushels of wheat.
At the present time we have our representatives sitting down in Washington trying to get another world wheat agreement. The people who are buying this wheat, especially the British, know perfectly well that this overhang on the world market is there. It cannot be explained away. The figures are right out in the open, and they know it is there. The British feel that, if we have no further wheat agreement, we might get back to the old system under which, if they bought wheat at the proper time, they would get it at a good cheap price; and a goodly number of the other importing countries know the same thing.
As long as we retain our wheat board and other selling countries deal in bulk, we have a certain advantage. The people of these various countries are financing the carryover of this wheat. But we can push that advantage just so far. The people of Canada are certainly not going to maintain a carryover of 550 million bushels of wheat in Canada for X number of years, and finance it. We have to put that wheat on the market.
So we come to dealing in price. I am a farmer and I certainly would like to see the highest possible price we can get. But on the other hand, as a farmer I certainly do not want to go back to the position of the thirties, where we demand a price that the importing countries are not prepared to pay and we keep our wheat in our elevators. That is no good to anybody. We are not even doing our duty because all over the world there are hungry mouths that want to eat wheat and wheat flour. It is our duty as a nation to see that we put that wheat in those peoples' mouths, at prices they can afford to pay. I certainly would not be a party to saying that we have to have $2.05, as was suggested here once this afternoon, or $2.17 or some other price, and that if we did not get it we would not sign the wheat agreement and we would not put wheat on the world market; because by doing so we would get ourselves caught in exactly the same trap in which we got ourselves caught in the thirties.
I have heard plenty of people say that the farmers of western Canada have lost millions and millions of dollars, or hundreds of
3216	HOUSE OF
Position of Agricultural Industry millions of dollars. Then they have compared our position to the United States position. The Americans eat 80 per cent of the wheat they grow; we have to sell 80 per cent of ours on the world market, and we have to be amenable to the conditions of the world market at the time.
I know perfectly well from the correspondence I get and from information I have received that the farmers in my constituency want to retain the wheat board. They have not been impressed by the arguments we have heard in the house and in other places against that board.
Where did you hear it?

From not very far away. The farmers also know that if we are going to retain the wheat board and if the people of Canada are going to continue to support it, then we are going to have to do it by getting a world wheat agreement. And we have to get that world wheat agreement at a price that importing nations are prepared to pay. I am certainly in favour of getting the highest possible price; but on the other hand I, as the member for Kindersley, would certainly not be prepared to take the responsibility for setting prices on our wheat at a point where we could not get the wheat agreement, or could not retain the wheat board.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, hon. members who have spoken so far in this debate have emphasized the contention that agricultural conditions and prices ought to be discussed at this particular time. I do not know just why they have conceived that idea all at once, particularly in view of the intimation by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair), who spoke a few moments ago on behalf of the Social Credit party, that this was the third time he had made a similar speech this session.
Just a minute. I said I got up three times.
Three times this afternoon.
That is worse.
Yes; that is even worse than I thought it was.
There was a little obstruction, that is all.

Nevertheless, it is about the third time similar speeches have been made by hon. members at this session. Therefore I cannot conceive of any good reason why it should be done again today, particularly
(Mr. Larson.1

in view of the fact that it is only a short time until we must have two occasions upon which we can discuss agricultural prices, and do so without interfering in any way with the general desire of the house to get along with the business.
One of those occasions is when the supplementary estimates for this year will be under consideration. A very considerable part of those estimates relate to agriculture, and have to do with this particular matter of prices. Another occasion will be when the estimates for the department are being considered. And if it requires even a third occasion, in all probability there will be further supplementary estimates for the coming year.
In other words we do not expect to be in session all summer. As a matter of fact I think it is anticipated by most hon. members that we will not be in session very long. And since we have three opportunities between now and the end of the session to discuss agricultural matters, I cannot conceive of any good reason why we ought to be discussing such matters at this time. So if hon. members had not been in the frame of mind where they thought it necessary to say some of the things they have said, I would not be making a speech this evening on this question.
Then again, I noticed that during the afternoon the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) was very busy, I presume organizing the debate for the afternoon and evening; because as each one on the other side of the house was interviewed he seemed to think it was necessary to make a speech, and got up and made one. The hon. member is free to do that if he so desires; but the thing that surprises me is that I have in my hand a letter he sent to his constituents. It was sent to me by a gentleman from out there who seems to think I ought to be informed as to what the hon. member is sending to his constituents. As a matter of fact I was familiar with some of this information before, because he has discussed some of these matters in the house. However, his letter contains some statements which have a bearing upon what we are discussing this evening. He says:
Dear Friend:
Saskatchewan's representation has been reduced from 20 to 17 members of parliament: but when Saskatchewan has only 17 members out of a total of 265 it is more essential than ever that each of those 17 members be a spokesman for the west.
I believe as a western member it is my duty to fight with courage, vigour and persistence, on your behalf. In carrying out this conviction some members have said "You talk too much" but let me tell you that as long as I am your member I will take second place to no one as a strong champion of the west.

And then his next paragraph:
I am enclosing information on farm income tax, and also a record of how the members voted on a number of motions of great importance to the people of Saskatchewan. While these motions did not receive the support that I suggested they deserved, nevertheless by pressing for better agricultural policies we have obtained some important concessions from the government.
For example, final payments for wheat, oats and barley are now being made a few months after the close of each crop year. We have also secured the continuance of the wheat board as the marketing agency for wheat and coarse grains.
If we are to achieve stability in livestock marketing we need a livestock board, a board of livestock commissioners and new trade policies to regain the British market. If a handful of members fighting for the west are able to secure valuable stability in grain marketing, a larger number of such members will be the best guarantee that stability will be obtained for the livestock industry.
Well, my hon. friend seems to think he has done such a good job in promoting the welfare of agriculture that I can hardly conceive of a good reason why he should have been so busy this afternoon working to organize a debate in which it is suggested that farmers are not doing very well. I am inclined to agree pretty well with what the letter says, in so far as stating the position in relation to agriculture is concerned; but I am not in agreement with the hon. member when he says that he has accomplished all these things.
I did not say that.

And I am quite sure that even the gentleman who sent this letter in to me and who happens to be a voter in his constituency, did not agree with it either. I will probably find that a great many others are in much the same classification.
I listened this afternoon to the speech delivered by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). He quoted from a speech which I made in 1945. I might take up the time of the house in order to quote from some speeches which he made.
Oh, don't do that.

No, I am not going to do that. If I were in the mood to do so I might quote speeches that have been made by some C.C.F. members, or probably I should say by those who used to be C.C.F. members in this house. The reason that speech was made in 1945 was that we were having an election, and the reason the other speeches were made in 1945 was the same.
I was suggesting to farmers at the time that they had not done too badly under a Liberal government from the time the war had started down to 1945. As a matter of fact I said to them what has been suggested by hon. members on a number of occasions,
Position of Agricultural Industry that if after putting us in they found that by the end of the four or five-year period it was proved to them that the statements made by our opponents to the effect that prices were going to go down and down were not wrong, I probably would not be a candidate four years later.
You know what happened in Saskatchewan. We had 19 out of 21 members ejected at that time in opposition to the government. Then we had four years' experience with the speech which I made and the speeches which my friends opposite made; at the end of that time we had 20 members instead of 21 from the province, and we elected 14 of them. Why? Because the farmers and others in Saskatchewan realized that the statements made in 1945 by us were correct, that every year from 1945 to 1949 there was a continuous increase in the prices obtained for farm products and not the reductions that had been prophesied by those of the opposition who were making speeches at that time.
I have no doubt that the prices of farm products will go up and come down from time to time. It will be possible to take different years when they are down and compare them with other years, just as it is possible to say that prices were down in 1952 as compared with 1951 and that they are probably down slightly again on some products in 1953 as compared with 1952. But when one takes the prices of farm products over a period of years and considers what is happening in relation to them it is absolutely impossible to show from any set of statistics that agricultural prices have been going down in the years since the war.
That is not the case. Agricultural prices for any period of years up to three that one wishes to take and compare with the last three years, let us say, of the war or the first three years after the war, have been going higher and higher in each period. It is just as true to say that the prices of everything else have been going higher and higher.
I am quite sure that if that were not right there would be a lot more people kicking in this country than there are at the present time. The fact of the matter is that what is needed in this or any other country is a set of returns for labour, for primary products and for food products which compare favourably. If one set of prices is rising it is good to have the other prices rising at the same time. If they rise comparably there is not very much to kick about.
All of us will be getting along fairly well. The only time the farmer can get along fairly well is when we have a condition vice versa to what has been described this afternoon by every speaker. Everyone who has got up

Position of Agricultural Industry has said that if we are going to have good times in this country, the farmer must be doing well. I am going to reverse that and say that if the farmer is going to be able to do well, everybody else has to be doing well. After all, what the farmer does is produce food and clothing for people. If the people are able to feed themselves reasonably well and clothe themselves reasonably well, if they can pay for the food and clothing that they eat and wear, then the farmers are going to do all right. As the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge) who started this debate this afternoon said, we are all interdependent in a country like Canada; we depend upon one another for the prosperity which we have. If those who are producing food products are going to be prosperous we must have the other people in the country doing fairly well on the wages they get.
I agree with the hon. member when he says that there is a great deal in common between labouring and farm people. If one group is going to be able to get along well the other must be able to get along well. Most of the people who live in Canada are either farmers or labouring people. All of them eat food. We can only have reasonably good prices for our farm products when the greater part of our population is able to pay reasonably good prices.
But our friends opposite seem to think that the principal method by which you can check whether prices are good or bad is on what they call a parity basis. The only objection I have to the word "parity" is that I seldom know what people mean when they use it.
They don't, either.

I do not understand what they are really talking about when they use the word. When I am discussing it I try to use terms which are a little different. As someone said this evening, I have said that I do not like the word "parity". I think it was the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) who said that. When I am explaining what I am speaking about I prefer to say that prices bear a reasonable relationship to the cost of the commodity.
In a few words that is what is meant; but even if we do take the word which my friends like to use, I would say that this evening and at other times they spend the greater part of their time in contending that we should have parity prices and then arguing that it should be the same as they have in the United States. Parity prices are always based upon some particular period of time. The United States took 1909-14 and they considered the conditions in the United States,

not in Canada or in Great Britain or somewhere else. They figured out their parity upon that basis.
At the time of a farm meeting in Niagara Falls three or four years ago we had a long discussion on this matter. One of the experts on matters of this kind who were there was Dr. Hope. There was present another expert on the same line from the United States; I think his name was Galbraith. There were others as well. Finally they all agreed that a parity based upon 1943, 1944 and 1945 would be much more in the interests of farmers in both countries than a parity based upon 1909 to 1914.
Our support prices and the price levels which result from the fact that we have support prices are based upon 1943, 1944 and 1945, as hon. members know and understand. Taking those and dealing with them in the same way the Americans do, United States support is 90 per cent of parity based upon 1909-14. Parity based upon 1943-45 would be much more helpful to farmers in that country and this country. One of the difficulties that some people find in connection with the matters is that they look at our price support and say that it is lower than United States price support. They say ours has not as high a parity value. As a matter of fact that is not what the experts say about it and it is not what they think about it, either.
Therefore I should like to point out what the position is in Canada, taking 90 per cent of parity based upon the three years I have mentioned with reference to Canadian prices and applying it to the last three years. The support price of butter was 58 cents a pound, No. 1, Montreal. The price obtained for butter was 61-6 cents a pound. Ninety per cent of parity would have been 56 cents. In other words, over the last three years the farm population has had a price 5 [DOT] 6 cents above parity worked out on the same basis in Canada, taking 1943, 1944 and 1945 as the basis.

I wonder if I might ask the minister a question. In his calculation of the parity price, has his 1943-45 base been adjusted upward to take care of the 60 point increase in the dominion bureau of statistics cost of production index?

Oh, all that is considered in arriving at any parity figure, and I assume our experts in Canada are just as good figurers as the same type of men in the United States. As a matter of fact the gentleman I spoke of a few moments ago was hired in Canada by the Americans and taken down there because they considered him a little better than anything they had at home. Therefore

I think our men probably do the figuring all right and take all the facts into consideration. When I say parity, it covers the same factors as in the United States.
If I might ask another question, what increase was taken into account in the new parity price for butter because of the increased cost of production?
We put the officials to work on it for us and this is the result of their work.
There was no consideration given.
Another false statement.

The support price on hogs was $26 to $27 a hundredweight. The actual price received over the three years was $30.60 a hundredweight. Ninety per cent of parity would have been $23. There was no support price on cattle in those three years, 1949, 1950 and 1951, but there was in 1952. It was $25 a hundredweight at Toronto. The price received in those three years averaged $26.45 a hundredweight. Ninety per cent of parity would have been $15.20 a hundredweight. The support price for wheat in 1949, 1950 and 1951 was $1.40 a bushel. That was the initial payment. The actual price in the basic years averaged $1.53. The actual price received in 1949, 1950 and 1951 was $1.84 a bushel, basis No. 1 northern, Fort William.
I give these figures in order to indicate that we are not in a bad position in Canada even on a parity basis as related to people in other countries. So I would say that we are not doing ourselves or the country in general any particular good by shouting to the world all the time that this is really a bad country in which to be farming. This has not been a bad country in which to be farming during the last ten or twelve years. There were times when we experienced great difficulty, but we have not been experiencing as great difficulty in recent years. Every farmer in the house knows that. He is not fooling even himself when he gets up here and makes statements to the contrary.
As a matter of fact I was in the city of Regina about a week ago and addressed the most representative group of farmers that ever meets in Saskatchewan. The same type of farmer meets in other provinces. I refer to the municipal associations. The municipal association of Saskatchewan is an association representing over 300 municipalities, and those municipalities are all rural. There were 1,200 delegates from those municipalities, and I had the privilege of speaking to them. I made a statement to them that I am going to make here now, and all I got from them
Position of Agricultural Industry when I made it was applause. I said to them: Every one of you men, all of whom are levying and collecting taxes, knows that the farmers of this province are in a better position to pay their taxes at present than they ever were at any previous time. I am quite sure that all the people who were at the gathering were not Liberals, but so far as I could see they practically all applauded; and I do not know any reason why members of the opposition should not applaud now, because that is the fact. Not only in Saskatchewan but in every part of Canada farmers are in a better position at present to pay their taxes than ever before.
You know, the letter of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) which I quoted has a very amusing table on the back of it. It has to do with taxes, and it arrives at some conclusions by a very peculiar method.
A devious method.

It takes a province like Saskatchewan, where 17 to 18 per cent of the farmers are able to pay income tax, figures out how much income tax they did pay, divides the farming population into the income tax they paid, and shows that on the average the farmers pay such and such. Then it takes the province of Quebec. Anybody who has ever travelled through the province of Quebec and through the province of Saskatchewan knows that by no stretch of the imagination could anything like the same percentage of farmers pay income tax in Quebec as do in Saskatchewan.
That is not saying anything which is detrimental to either Saskatchewan or Quebec. As I understand it, the average size farm in the province of Quebec is 65 acres. The average size farm in Saskatchewan is something approaching 300 acres. It is not the kind of farm that is talked about by some people in the house when they are discussing the west. They talk about the west as though we all lived on farms of anywhere from two sections up to ten sections. People are continuously talking that way, but as a matter of fact I believe that only about 1J per cent of the farmers of Saskatchewan live on farms that are two sections or more. We nearly all live on half-section farms, a half-section being 320 acres, and most of us who do not live on half-section farms live on three-quarter section farms. There are a great many fewer living on three-quarter section farms and, in any case, on an average the cultivated acreage of farms in Saskatchewan is something under 300 acres.
The greater number of those who pay the income tax that is spoken of are the com-

Position of Agricultural Industry paratively few who live on the greater acreages. I would say that the comparison which ought to be made between Saskatchewan and Quebec is the comparison between the farmer who lives on a half section in the west and the farmer who lives on 3 100-acre farm in the province of Quebec. I think the same kind of comparison would be absolutely fair as between the farmer living in Ontario and the farmer living in the western part of Canada.

I shall be glad to hear my good friend the hon. member for Maple Creek get up and tell us how prosperous his farmers are, how satisfied they are under present conditions, and whether they have any concern for the immediate future.
They still appreciate correct figures.

They are government figures and I cannot vouch for them. There is another great problem in this country which affects the eastern farmer particularly. A great deal of money has been spent over the past years on freight assistance on feed
Position of Agricultural Industry grain coming east for use by eastern feeders. The taxpayer is paying that. There is great dissatisfaction among these eastern feeders over the cost of these feed grains at the present time, and the grades they are able to obtain.
Are you in favour of paying that subsidy?
Make your own speech.

I should like to hear the new independent Liberal member for Springfield make a speech on behalf of the farmers whom he may be representing in the next parliament.
I am not able to find out where the trouble is in connection with this feed grain proposition, but I submit that the chairman of the committee on agriculture and colonization should call the committee together and have the officials of the Canadian wheat board before it so we can try to get to the root of this difficulty. There is something radically wrong, and I am not able to put my finger on the difficulty. I am satisfied that the spread between the cost to the eastern feeder and what the western producer receives is altogether too great. I am not sure whether we could obtain the necessary information from the officials of the Canadian wheat board, but I think the government owes it both to the producers and the eastern feeders to try to find out what is the cause of the great disparity and to seek a solution for this most vexing problem. Despite the cost to the taxpayers of the country, the situation is most unsatisfactory at the present time.
I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) if he would refer the 1951-52 Canadian wheat board report to the committee on agriculture and colonization, and he stated that he would do so if it was the desire of the committee. You will realize, Mr. Speaker, that all our committees have a large majority of supporters of the government; and interpreting his answer as I find it in Hansard I presume it will depend on whether or not the majority on the committee on agriculture wish to do that. In fairness to feeders and producers alike I think it should be done. I do not know of any better approach at this time, and I sincerely ask that this at least should be done.
I think the production of hogs in this country has been done an injustice, because many people have gone out of hog production. My good friend the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth (Mr. Charlton) had a question on the order paper the other day about canned pork. I have not all the facts before me, but I can say that it was pointed out that since March, 1952 the government had

Position of Agricultural Industry bought some 94 million pounds of pork for canning, had sold some 21 million pounds, and was still holding a surplus of approximately 73 million pounds at the present time.
Who got the subsidy?

So far as beef is concerned, the minister pointed out that the Canadian market is still very good, but there was a reduction during the past year of 37 and a fraction per cent in the price of cattle.
I am not stating that prices had not been very high previously.
In general the farm producer is very fearful of the immediate future so far as the products he has to sell are concerned, whether it be dairy products, fruit, vegetables, meat or cereals, because he is going to be asked to take less than he has been getting for them while his costs are going up in every respect and are likely to go up for some time. The estimates of the agricultural division of the bureau of statistics for the coming year indicate that in all likelihood the cost of production for the farm producer will increase and that in general he will be asked to take less for his products.
So far as floor prices for agricultural products are concerned, it was announced as the policy of this party some years ago that we were in favour of floor prices. I presume that is still our policy. Therefore I support

the amendment to the motion to go into supply. I am satisfied that the vast majority of agricultural producers from coast to coast want some assurance as to what their situation will be in the year ahead. That is particularly important in the case of our prairie farmers, who will now be making arrangements for their spring production.

The public will never swallow that bait.
On motion of Mr. Wright the debate was adjourned.
